explain.say: Some redwood trees in California are taller than a 30-storey building, yet they have no heart and no pump. So how does water get from the roots to the very top leaves? Let's follow one drop.

explain.say: Start at the bottom, at the root hairs. Water from the soil moves into them by osmosis, which means water soaking from a dilute place into a more concentrated one. Then it moves across the root to the xylem. Where does it go next?

explain.say: Now look up the trunk. The xylem is made of thin, hollow tubes. Water sticks together and to the tube walls, so it forms one long, unbroken thread, all the way up. Have you ever sucked a drink up a straw?

explain.say: See the stomata on the leaves? Water evaporates inside the leaf and escapes as vapour through these tiny pores. This loss is called transpiration. Each molecule that leaves tugs the next one up behind it. Can you picture the chain?

explain.say: That constant flow from roots to leaves is the transpiration stream. Fantastic! Wow fact: a big oak tree can lose over 100 litres of water on a hot summer day, mostly through its leaves.

faq.q: How does water get into the root hairs?
faq.a: By osmosis. The cell sap inside the root hair is more concentrated than the soil water, so water moves into the cell through its partially permeable membrane.
asks: Tell me about the root hairs

faq.q: How does water travel up the trunk?
faq.a: In xylem vessels. Water molecules cling to each other, called cohesion, and to the vessel walls, so evaporation at the leaves pulls an unbroken column of water upwards.
asks: Tell me about the xylem in the trunk

faq.a: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly by evaporation from cells inside the leaves and diffusion out through the stomata.
Higher temperature, more light (which opens stomata), wind that blows vapour away, and dry air all speed up transpiration. Humid, still, cool air slows it.
asks: What affects the rate of transpiration?

faq.a: It brings water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves, keeps cells firm, and cools the plant as water evaporates.

facts: The tallest known living tree, a coast redwood called Hyperion, is about 116 metres tall.
Water moves up xylem as a continuous column held together by cohesion between water molecules.
